title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm that solves every rational P-matrix linear complementarity problem in polynomial bit time? More precisely, are there a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded rational input
\[n\in\mathbb N_{>0},\qquad M\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad q\in\mathbb Q^n,\]
the machine halts within \(B(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below, and whenever \(M\) is a P-matrix it outputs \(z,w\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying
\[w=Mz+q,\qquad z_i\ge0,\quad w_i\ge0,\quad z_iw_i=0\quad(1\le i\le n)?\]
A P-matrix has strictly positive determinant for every nonempty principal submatrix. No certificate of this promise is supplied, and the algorithm need not recognize it. The constants \(B,k\) and the program are shared by all dimensions and all rational coefficients.
definitions:
Matrix promise. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), the principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) consists of the rows and columns with indices in \(S\), both in increasing order. Thus the promise is
\[\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n],\ \det M[S,S]>0.\]
Here the determinant is the usual alternating sum of products, evaluated exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). Strict positivity is essential. There is no symmetry, sparsity, triangularity, positive-semidefiniteness or nondegeneracy assumption. In particular, a valid solution may have both \(z_i=w_i=0\) in some coordinate.

Equations and output. The matrix product is \((Mz)_i=\sum_{j=1}^nM_{ij}z_j\), and all inequalities use the ordinary rational order. With \(z,w\ge0\), coordinatewise complementarity is equivalent to \(z^Tw=\sum_{i=1}^n z_iw_i=0\). A solution is the complete pair of vectors, with exact rational coordinates. An interval, floating-point vector or small residual is not an exact solution under this task. The guarantee is a search guarantee: returning only a yes/no answer about existence is insufficient.

Binary encoding. To make the bit model definite, encode a nonnegative integer \(t\) by
\[u(t)=1^{b(t)}0\,\operatorname{bin}(t+1),\qquad b(t)=\lfloor\log_2(t+1)\rfloor+1,\]
where \(\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) is its binary expansion without leading zeroes, of length \(b(t)\). The initial run of ones specifies that length. A rational number is written uniquely as \(p/d\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) and \(\gcd(|p|,d)=1\), and is encoded by a sign bit, then \(u(|p|)\), then \(u(d)\). The sign bit is zero for nonnegative \(p\), including zero, and one for negative \(p\). Thus zero uses numerator zero and denominator one. The input concatenates \(u(n)\), all \(n^2\) entries of \(M\) in row-major order, and the \(n\) entries of \(q\). Every entry, including a zero entry, is explicitly present. A syntactically valid input has exactly this form and no trailing bits. Its total binary length is \(N\). The output concatenates the \(n\) rational encodings of \(z\), followed by those of \(w\), in index order; \(n\) is already known from the input. Other usual explicit binary rational encodings are polynomially equivalent to this convention.

Computation. The same finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program is used for every input. One transition costs one step. Reading input, rational arithmetic, comparisons, intermediate representations and writing the entire output are all charged. There are no oracles, real-number unit-cost operations, randomness, nonuniform advice or free preprocessing. The polynomial time bound applies to every syntactically valid rational input, including matrices that fail the P-matrix promise. On those nonpromised inputs any halting output is allowed; detecting a violated principal minor is not required. Behavior on malformed input strings is unrestricted. A polynomial bound only on promised inputs is equivalent for this existence question, since a known polynomial bound can be enforced with a clock and arbitrary output after timeout. The bound may depend polynomially on coefficient bit lengths through \(N\); this is not a demand for a strongly polynomial number of arithmetic operations independent of those lengths.

Quantifier order. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists B,k\,\forall(n,M,q)\) with the time guarantee above and correctness whenever \(\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\). Coefficient magnitudes, dimension, degeneracy and numerical conditioning may vary without restriction; they do not permit selecting a different program or polynomial for each input.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this algorithm-existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish one program, one polynomial bit-time bound and exact correctness on every promised input, including degenerate instances. Any internal approximation procedure must be proved to recover and output the exact rational solution within that bound. A negative answer must show that every uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs fails to output the required solution on some P-matrix instance. Exponential examples for one pivot rule, hardness of recognizing P-matrices, a lower bound in a restricted oracle model, or a conditional complexity-theoretic barrier alone do not prove that negation. An algorithm for a proper matrix subclass or with an uncontrolled condition-parameter factor does not establish the positive answer.
why: The P-matrix promise guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side, and that solution has a short rational description. The remaining difficulty is finding it efficiently despite the coupled choices of which coordinates vanish. A polynomial algorithm would resolve a central structured search problem that sits between tractable linear optimization and more general complementarity systems.

importance.reason: A longstanding general optimization question with a strong total-search interpretation and continuing work on both structural and algorithmic restrictions. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity, distinct from strong polynomiality of LP and exact SDP feasibility.

progress.text: Murty characterizes P-matrices through existence of a unique complementarity solution for every right-hand side.
Gärtner and Sprecher give polynomial algorithms for tridiagonal and, more generally, Hessenberg P-matrices.
The Unique End of Potential Line preprint gives promise-preserving reductions for P-LCP; the work later appeared at ICALP2019 and in JCSS2020.
Gordon and Shu make several non-P-matrix certificate forms polynomially interconvertible. This concerns violated promises, not a general solution algorithm.
Polynomial reductions identify generalized P-LCP with its ordinary binary-choice form.
ETH’s activity report retains polynomial-time general P-matrix LCP as an unresolved question.
The revised handicap-reduction paper improves algorithmic dependence to the best value under positive diagonal scaling. Its theorem retains a parameter beyond input length.

context_blocks.text: Complementarity imposes a discrete choice within linear equations: each coordinate must have \(z_i=0\), or \(w_i=0\), or both. For \(M=I_n\), the solution is \(z_i=\max\{0,-q_i\}\) and \(w_i=\max\{0,q_i\}\). For a general P-matrix, the coordinates interact through \(Mz\), so this coordinate-by-coordinate formula no longer applies.

The classical P-matrix characterization states that the linear complementarity system has exactly one solution for every real right-hand side if and only if all principal minors are positive. Uniqueness concerns the vector pair, not the choice of a complementary basis; degenerate instances can have several bases representing the same solution. The existence and uniqueness theorem does not itself give the polynomial algorithm requested here.

Rational exact output does not require an exponentially long description. In a solution, let \(S=\{i:z_i>0\}\). Then \(z_{[n]\setminus S}=0\), \(w_S=0\), and \(M[S,S]z_S=-q_S\); this principal matrix is nonsingular. Clearing input denominators and applying determinant bounds shows that its rational solution and the resulting \(w\) have polynomial bit length. If \(S\) is empty, \(z=0\) and \(w=q\). The difficult part is finding a valid pattern efficiently.

P-matrix recognition is co-NP-complete, but this card supplies the property as a promise. Gordon and Shu give polynomial conversions between different certificates that a matrix violates the promise. Such certificate results do not make recognition part of this task, and recognition hardness does not prove that promised solution finding is hard.

Fearnley, Gordon, Mehta and Savani place the promised problem in a class based on finding the endpoint of a unique, implicitly represented path whose potential increases along it. Their total-search variants permit a certificate of a violated promise as an alternative output. These complexity-class containments organize the search problem but do not give polynomial-time solution finding. The present card requires a solution only on P-matrix inputs.

Gärtner and Sprecher give polynomial algorithms for Hessenberg P-matrices, which have zero entries beyond the first off-diagonal on one side; tridiagonal matrices are included. Their \(O(n^5)\) arithmetic-operation bound combines polynomially many basis tests with linear-system solves. Exact rational linear algebra gives polynomial bit complexity for these subclasses. The general matrix in this card has no such zero pattern.

The ICALP 2024 paper “Two Choices Are Enough” reduces generalized complementarity instances to the ordinary binary-choice problem and relates them to geometric search problems. This equivalence extends the reach of P-matrix LCP; it is not a polynomial solver for it. ETH’s 2025 activity report continues to list general polynomial-time solution finding as open.

E.-Nagy and Végh’s June 2026 revision gives an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the input length and in the optimized handicap \(\widehat\kappa^\star(M)\), the best handicap attainable by positive diagonal row scaling. The handicap measures departure from the inequality \(x^TMx\ge0\). Their general upper bound on the unscaled handicap is exponential in input bit complexity, and the algorithmic theorem does not give a polynomial input-length bound on the optimized parameter. It therefore does not settle the all-P-matrix target.

source_formulation.text: The retained question is ordinary deterministic polynomial bit-time solution of rational LCP under the P-matrix promise. It asks neither for recognizing that promise nor for a strongly polynomial arithmetic algorithm. The literature’s unique-sink and total-search formulations supply context; they do not add an obligation to produce non-P-matrix certificates here.

sentences: The problem asks for nonnegative rational vectors linked by a linear equation, with at least one zero in each paired coordinate.
The input matrix is promised to have every nonempty principal minor strictly positive, which guarantees a unique solution for every right-hand side.
The question is whether one deterministic algorithm always finds that exact solution in polynomial time measured in the full binary input length.
A complete Lean proof must supply that uniform algorithm and bound or rule out every such polynomial-time algorithm without adding a promise-recognition task.
The checked 2026 handicap-dependent algorithm and earlier restricted-matrix and reduction results do not establish this general polynomial-time guarantee.
